summary: TALI – Integrated Health and Life Support System is a technological innovation initiative focused on developing an intelligent medical monitoring and support system for astronauts during space missions. It integrates biometric sensors, cardiac and pulmonary ultrasound imaging, 12-lead electrocardiography, and continuous vital sign monitoring. By leveraging artificial intelligence, the system generates early warning alerts, predictive models, and clinical decision-support tools for environments where direct medical assistance is unavailable.
details:
Project TALI (Integrated Health and Life Support System) is a biomedical system embedded directly into an intelligent spacesuit, engineered to deliver advanced life support and autonomous clinical decision-making during space missions where medical personnel are absent. Its acronym reflects its core functional architecture: T (Telemetry of vital signs), A(Aerospace context / microgravity), L (advanced Life support), and I (Integration of diagnostic data and imaging via Artificial Intelligence).

What does it do?

Continuous physiological monitoring: Tracks vital signs in real time (heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation / SpO2 respiratory rate, and body temperature).

Advanced ultrasound and electrocardiography: Captures diagnostic ultrasound imaging of the heart, thorax, and inferior vena cava, along with a full 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG).

Predictive clinical risk evaluation: Logs biomedical parameters to compute early warning scores (such as the NEWS2 score).

AI-driven clinical decision support: Runs predictive models and algorithms that analyze incoming data to propose diagnoses and therapeutic pathways directly to the crew.

How does it work?

The system operates across three interconnected layers built into the spacesuit architecture:

1. Sensor-Based Data Capture in the Spacesuit

Piezoelectric sensors: Embedded across the suit to execute automated point-of-care ultrasound protocols:

FoCUS Protocol (Focused Cardiac Ultrasound): Evaluates left ventricular systolic function and contractility, ventricular size and chamber ratio (detecting right ventricular strain or the "D-sign" characteristic of pulmonary embolism), pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade, and inferior vena cava collapsibility to estimate central venous pressure and fluid responsiveness.

BLUE Protocol (Bedside Lung Ultrasound in Emergency): Differentiates etiologies of acute dyspnea by identifying lung profiles (Profile A for asthma/COPD; Profile B for cardiogenic pulmonary edema; Profile C for pneumonia/consolidations; lung point identification to rule in/out pneumothorax, and pleural effusion detection).

12-lead ECG electrodes: Continuously analyze cardiac rhythm, P/T wave morphology, QRS complexes, and ST segments to detect arrhythmias, ischemia/infarction, or electrolyte imbalances.

Finger probe sensor (photoplethysmography, multispectral optical spectrophotometry, and pulse CO-oximetry): Measures systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial pressure, cardiac output, stroke volume variation, pulse pressure variation, total hemoglobin, and SpO2

2. Processing and Artificial Intelligence Core

Integrated and external transceivers: Aggregate incoming telemetry, store historical health data, and run AI algorithms to cross-correlate ultrasound imagery, ECG tracings, and hemodynamics. Based on these inputs, the system generates differential diagnoses and suggests clinical management protocols.

3. User Interface (Forearm Display)

Forearm-mounted display: Enables the astronaut to monitor individual or combined physiological parameters in real time, inspect trends over time, and immediately read diagnostic findings and clinical action steps formulated by the AI

[10:30 p. m., 15/11/2026] Carlos Fernando Reyes Martinez: Project TALI, here are the key benefits the system offers:

Autonomous medical care without specialists: Provides advanced life support and direct clinical assistance to the crew in deep-space environments where flight surgeons or medical specialists are not physically present.   

Early deterioration detection & predictive risk scoring: Continuously logs physiological telemetry to calculate standardized early warning scores (such as the NEWS2 score), identifying clinical decline before symptoms become critical.  

AI-guided clinical decision support: Employs predictive models and algorithms that cross-analyze biomedical data, propose differential diagnoses, and recommend tailored therapeutic interventions in real time.   

Suit-integrated cardiopulmonary ultrasound & diagnostics:   

FoCUS protocol: Assesses left ventricular systolic function and contractility, identifies pericardial effusions or cardiac tamponade, flags ventricular strain / pulmonary embolism (D-shaped septum), and evaluates inferior vena cava collapsibility for volume responsiveness.   

BLUE protocol: Rapidly differentiates acute dyspnea causes (distinguishing asthma/COPD, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and pneumonia/consolidations), rules in or out pneumothorax, and detects pleural effusions.  

Continuous 12-lead ECG: Detects cardiac arrhythmias, acute ischemia or infarction, and signs of electrolyte imbalances directly from embedded electrodes.  

Continuous non-invasive hemodynamic monitoring: Uses an integrated finger probe (photoplethysmography, pulse CO-oximetry, and optical spectrophotometry) to track continuous blood pressure (systolic, diastolic, and mean), cardiac output, stroke volume variation, pulse pressure variation, total hemoglobin, and SpO2      

Direct real-time feedback for the astronaut: The forearm display allows the crew member to inspect individual or combined vital parameters, track temporal trends, and immediately read diagnostic findings and clinical steps without interrupting operational tasks.

[10:30 p. m., 15/11/2026] Carlos Fernando Reyes Martinez: The ability to obtain information on physiological variables in real time—both on Earth and in zero gravity—enables the monitoring of physiological changes and adaptation during the transition from Earth to space.

The TALI Project stands out for its creative and innovative approach in various aspects of biomedical engineering and aerospace medicine:

Embedding diagnostic imaging directly into the spacesuit: Instead of requiring external, bulky ultrasound equipment that the astronaut must manipulate, it integrates piezoelectric sensors distributed throughout the suit itself. This automates the capture of advanced real-time ultrasounds under recognized clinical protocols such as FoCUS (cardiac and vena cava) and BLUE (pulmonary). 

Multimodal integration of data and medical vision: It combines in a single architecture continuous physiological telemetry (heart rate, temperature, SpO2 ), a complete 12-lead electrocardiogram, advanced vascular parameters via a finger sensor (co-oximetry, multispectral optical spectrophotometry, and photoplethysmography), and diagnostic ultrasound images.  

Clinical autonomy guided by Artificial Intelligence: It is designed to solve the physical absence of physicians or specialists on space missions. The AI not only compiles data, but also calculates early warning scores (such as the NEWS2 score), executes predictive models, and generates decision support algorithms to propose diagnoses and treatments to the crew.  

Ergonomic interface and immediate feedback (Forearm display): It incorporates a display mounted on the forearm of the suit so that the astronaut can visualize their variables individually or combined, review their temporal evolution, and directly access the AI's diagnostic recommendations without interrupting their operational maneuvers.

The TALI Project is creative and innovative primarily in how it transforms a conventional spacesuit into an autonomous and intelligent hospital, standing out in four essential aspects:

Textile integration of ultrasound diagnosis: Instead of requiring external ultrasound equipment that takes up space and demands specialized training to manipulate the probe, it integrates piezoelectric sensors directly into the suit's structure. This automates complex clinical protocols such as FoCUS (cardiac and vena cava evaluation) and BLUE (pulmonary pathologies) without manual intervention.

Multimodal fusion of clinical data: It connects into a single continuous ecosystem basic telemetry (temperature, respiratory rate, etc.), a complete 12-lead electrocardiogram, vascular hemodynamic monitoring via a finger sensor (co-oximetry, optical spectrophotometry, and photoplethysmography), and ultrasound imaging diagnostics.

Clinical autonomy with Artificial Intelligence: It is designed to operate in deep-space scenarios where there are no physicians on board and no immediate communication with Earth. The AI is not limited to collecting figures: it calculates standardized clinical risk scales (such as the NEWS2 score), executes predictive models, and issues differential diagnoses with therapeutic recommendations in real time.

Direct ergonomic feedback (Forearm Display): It incorporates a display on the forearm of the suit that allows the astronaut to monitor their individual or combined physiological metrics, track their temporal evolution, and immediately read the AI's indications without interrupting their activities or maneuvers in space

As a physician specializing in critical care, I sought to recreate an intensive care unit within a spacesuit, enabling the monitoring and storage of vital signs, laboratory data, and medical imaging. The goal was to understand how the human body adapts to zero gravity over extended periods and to establish new benchmarks for "normal" vital signs and physiological variables.
